title: Design a Distributed Unique ID Generator (Snowflake)
relevance: High — Alex Xu Vol.1 Ch.7 staple; shows up standalone and as a building block inside URL shortener, chat, news feed, booking; FAANG + Indian product cos probe Snowflake vs UUID vs ticket server.
company_notes: Campus/new-grad often as a short deep-dive inside URL shortener, feed, or chat, or a full 45-min for distributed-systems fundamentals; experienced (1–4 YOE) as standalone Snowflake or multi-DC ID service with probes on clock skew, ZK assignment, bit tuning, and UUID v7. Twitter/X origin; asked widely at Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Uber, Atlassian, Flipkart, etc. High-frequency building-block alongside URL shortener—know the 64-bit diagram cold.

phases.goal: Lock the ID contract: uniqueness, size/shape, ordering, QPS/latency, and what is out of scope.

must_hit.point: FR/NFR triad: globally unique, 64-bit numeric, roughly time-sortable IDs at ≥ 10k IDs/s, low latency, high availability, no single-writer SPOF
must_hit.evidence_hint: States nextId() must be unique + 64-bit + roughly time-ordered, cites ≥ 10k IDs/s and availability without a central writer

must_hit.point: Defend why UUID v4 fails (128-bit, not ordered) and ticket server fails (SPOF / bottleneck) against that triad
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly rejects UUID v4 on size/ordering and ticket server on SPOF/throughput before proposing Snowflake

must_hit.point: Clarify roughly time-ordered vs strict global monotonicity, multi-region needs, whether IDs must hide business volume, and out-of-scope items like cryptographic unguessability
must_hit.evidence_hint: Asks interviewer whether k-ordering is enough, multi-DC, sequential-leak concerns, and parks crypto/secondary indexes unless asked

probes: What properties must the IDs satisfy, and why isn't UUID v4 or a ticket server enough?

hints.1: Start from functional nextId() plus the usual non-functional constraints interviewers expect for an ID generator.
hints.2: Name the Alex Xu triad—unique, 64-bit numeric, roughly time-sortable—and the QPS bar, then knock out UUID v4 and ticket server.
hints.3: Say: unique + 64-bit + roughly time-sortable + ≥ 10k IDs/s + no SPOF; UUID v4 is 128-bit/unordered; ticket server is a central bottleneck.

phases.goal: Show capacity math: cluster target vs per-worker ceiling and timestamp lifetime.

must_hit.point: Alex Xu baseline ~10k IDs/s cluster-wide is far below one worker's theoretical ~4M IDs/s/worker; social/chat peaks of 100k–1M IDs/s still need only tens of workers
must_hit.evidence_hint: States 10k IDs/s baseline, notes one worker's ~4M IDs/s headroom, and maps 100k–1M peaks to tens of workers

must_hit.point: 41-bit millisecond timestamp from a custom epoch lasts ~69 years; per-worker ceiling is 2^12 × 1000 = 4,096,000 IDs/s
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites 41-bit ms → ~69 years and 12-bit sequence × 1000 ms → 4,096,000 IDs/s per worker

must_hit.point: If generation is local, CPU/clock—not a DB—is the bottleneck; network matters only for a remote ID service
must_hit.evidence_hint: Concludes local Snowflake is clock/CPU bound; networking appears only if IDs are fetched over RPC

probes: Walk through QPS and how long the timestamp field lasts—where does the system actually bottleneck?

hints.1: Pick a cluster QPS target out loud and compare it to one worker's capacity.
hints.2: Use the 41-bit ms lifetime (~69 years) and 12-bit sequence × 1000 for per-worker ceiling.
hints.3: Say ~10k IDs/s baseline vs ~4M IDs/s/worker (4,096,000); 41 bits ≈ 69 years; bottleneck is CPU/clock if local.

phases.goal: Define how callers get IDs—prefer library/sidecar, optional batched RPC and decode.

must_hit.point: Prefer library/sidecar APIs: long nextId() and List<Long> nextIds(int n) in-process to avoid per-ID network hops
must_hit.evidence_hint: Proposes nextId()/nextIds(n) embedded or on localhost rather than a remote hop per insert

must_hit.point: Optional RPC POST /v1/ids with count returning ids, plus GET /v1/ids/{id}/meta for timestamp/datacenter/worker/sequence; auth and rate-limit the network service
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows batched POST /v1/ids, optional meta decode, and notes auth/rate-limits on the networked path only

probes: How do clients call the generator—library vs service—and what does the interface look like?

hints.1: Decide first whether IDs are minted in-process or over the network.
hints.2: Sketch nextId/nextIds for the library path and a batched POST plus optional meta GET for RPC.
hints.3: Prefer long nextId() / nextIds(n); optional POST /v1/ids {count} → {ids}, GET .../meta with timestamp_ms, datacenter_id, worker_id, sequence; lock down the network path.

phases.goal: Model tiny local worker state and the classic 64-bit pack; persist only ID leases.

must_hit.point: IdWorker state: workerId 0..31, datacenterId 0..31, sequence 0..4095, lastTimestamp, with nextId, tilNextMillis, and timeGen
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those fields/ranges and the three methods as the in-memory worker model

must_hit.point: Classic pack: id = ((now - epoch) << 22) | (datacenterId << 17) | (workerId << 12) | sequence — i.e. 1 unused + 41 ts + 10 machine (often 5+5) + 12 sequence → 4096 IDs/ms/worker
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes the shift formula or equivalent 1+41+10+12 layout and 4096 IDs/ms/worker

must_hit.point: Persist only machine-ID assignment leases (ZooKeeper/etcd/config), not every generated ID
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says durable state is worker/datacenter assignment only; generated IDs stay ephemeral bit-packs

probes: What state does a worker keep, and how do you lay out the 64 bits?

hints.1: This is barely a DB design—focus on per-worker fields and the bit layout.
hints.3: IdWorker: ids 0..31 / 0..31, seq 0..4095, lastTimestamp; id = ((now-epoch)<<22)|(dc<<17)|(worker<<12)|seq; only leases are persisted.

phases.goal: Embed Snowflake locally with one-time worker-ID assignment; discard SPOF and unordered alternatives.

must_hit.point: App servers call a local Snowflake library/sidecar using NTP-synced clock, in-memory sequence, and a workerId assigned once
must_hit.evidence_hint: Draws App → local library with clock + sequence + workerId; prefers embed/sidecar over multi-hop microservice

must_hit.point: Uniqueness without per-ID coordination: unique machine ID at startup (ZooKeeper/etcd/config/IP/ordinal); generation is then local bit-pack
must_hit.evidence_hint: States coordination only at startup for workerId; each nextId is local clock+counter+pack

must_hit.point: Compare-and-discard: ticket server / Redis INCR path is SPOF/latency; UUID v4 local fails 64-bit + sort requirements; multi-DC encodes datacenterId with healthy NTP
must_hit.evidence_hint: Verbalizes discarded ticket/UUID paths and multi-DC via datacenterId + NTP

probes: Sketch the high-level design and what you deliberately are not building.

hints.1: Keep ID minting next to the app unless polyglot clients force a service.
hints.2: Show local generate path plus optional ZK/etcd startup lease; contrast ticket server and UUID v4.
hints.3: App → Snowflake library (clock, mutex sequence, workerId); startup lease for unique workerId; reject ticket SPOF and UUID v4; encode datacenterId for multi-DC.

phases.goal: Probe Snowflake vs alternatives, clock skew, worker-ID lifecycle, and bit-budget tuning.

must_hit.point: Snowflake vs ticket server vs UUID: Snowflake when you need 64-bit + time order + no per-ID coord; ticket server for strict global sequence/simplicity at low QPS; UUID v7/ULID when 128-bit is OK and you want zero machine-ID ops
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps each alternative to the requirement it wins on without claiming Snowflake always wins

must_hit.point: Clock skew is the hard problem: NTP step backward risks duplicates—refuse or wait until now > lastTimestamp; prefer forward-only slew; on sequence 4095 in the same ms, tilNextMillis
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes backward-clock wait/refuse, slew vs step, and spinning to next ms after sequence 4095

must_hit.point: Worker ID lifecycle: static config vs ZK/etcd ephemeral (auto reclaim, fence long GC/network blips) vs Instagram in-Postgres (41 ts + 13 shard + 10 seq); Discord uses 42-bit ts / 5 worker / 5 process / 12 incr and string JSON IDs
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares assignment strategies and cites Instagram/Discord layout differences without conflating them

must_hit.point: Bit-budget tuning: reallocate the 10 machine + 12 sequence bits (e.g. shrink DC bits, grow workers/sequence) for known topology
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows willingness to trade timestamp years vs workers vs per-ms burst for the stated topology

probes: When would you pick a ticket server or UUID v7 instead, and how do you handle clocks moving backwards?

hints.1: Interviewers usually push alternatives and failure modes next—clocks and worker IDs.
hints.2: Structure: requirement fit of Snowflake/ticket/UUID, then backward NTP handling, then how workerIds are assigned.
hints.3: Snowflake for 64-bit+order+local mint; ticket for strict sequence; UUID v7 if 128-bit OK; on skew wait/refuse until now > lastTimestamp; tune 10+12 bits; mention Instagram/Discord variants if asked.

phases.goal: Scale workers, handle hot shards and remote fetch, and protect uniqueness across failures/regions.

must_hit.point: Horizontal scale: add workers with new IDs—QPS scales linearly until the 10-bit (or tuned) machine space is exhausted
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says add workers for linear QPS until machine-ID bits run out

must_hit.point: Hot worker: >4k IDs/ms → wait for next ms, split processes (Discord-style process bits), or widen sequence; remote ID service should batch and prefetch ranges
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the >4k IDs/ms wait/split/widen path and batching/prefetch for RPC

must_hit.point: Failure/multi-region: worker death is fine; do not reassign workerId while its clock window could collide—wait out lease/max skew; regions stay independent with k-ordering only within NTP/network skew; time-leading IDs help B-tree locality vs UUID v4
must_hit.evidence_hint: Avoids eager workerId reuse, accepts cross-region ordering limits, and notes append-friendly inserts vs random UUIDs

probes: How does this scale under a hot worker or multi-region load, and what breaks uniqueness on failure?

hints.1: Think worker count, per-ms burst, and what happens when a worker dies.
hints.2: Cover linear add-workers, the >4k IDs/ms case, and lease/skew before workerId reuse.
hints.3: Add workers until 10-bit space ends; on >4k IDs/ms wait/split/widen; batch remote fetches; hold workerId past max skew; time-ordered inserts beat UUID v4 page splits.

tradeoffs.topic: Snowflake vs ticket server vs UUID
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Snowflake wins for 64-bit numeric, roughly time-ordered IDs with no per-ID coordination once workerIds exist. Ticket server (Flickr-style) wins for strict global sequence and simplicity at low QPS but is a SPOF/bottleneck unless carefully paired. UUID v4 needs no coordination but is 128-bit and unordered (hurts indexes); UUID v7/ULID keep sortability at 128-bit with zero machine-ID ops when 64-bit is not required.

tradeoffs.topic: Clock skew handling: wait/refuse vs logical offset
tradeoffs.strong_answer: On backward NTP steps, refuse or sleep until now > lastTimestamp so you never reuse a (timestamp, worker, seq) tuple; prefer NTP that slews forward-only. Same-ms IDs may interleave across machines by worker then sequence—usually acceptable k-ordering, not a Lamport clock. Sequence overflow at 4095 in one ms uses tilNextMillis.

tradeoffs.topic: Worker ID assignment: static vs ZK ephemeral vs in-DB shard
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Static config is simple but ops-heavy. ZK/etcd ephemeral leases auto-reclaim but must fence long GC and network blips so two live nodes never share an ID. Instagram bakes shard bits into Postgres (41+13+10) and skips a separate Snowflake fleet; Discord adds process bits and returns string IDs for JSON.

tradeoffs.topic: Bit-budget: timestamp years vs workers vs per-ms burst
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Classic 1+41+10+12 (~69 years, 4096 IDs/ms/worker). Tuning reallocates the 10 machine and 12 sequence bits for known topology (e.g. fewer DC bits, more workers or sequence) when years of timestamp headroom can be traded for capacity.

gotchas.trap: Clock moved backwards—keep minting with the old or new wall clock naively
gotchas.correction: Refuse or sleep until catch-up; never emit a duplicate (timestamp, worker, seq). Prefer NTP slew over step; optionally track last ID time.

gotchas.trap: Claiming IDs are strictly monotonic across the whole fleet
gotchas.correction: Only roughly time-ordered (Twitter aimed ~1s); same-ms order is by machine then sequence. Call them k-sorted, not a global Lamport clock.

gotchas.trap: Defaulting to UUID without checking requirements
gotchas.correction: UUID is 128-bit; v4 is random and hurts indexes. If 128-bit is allowed, prefer UUID v7 (RFC 9562) / ULID over v4.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Discord/Instagram are identical to classic Twitter Snowflake
gotchas.correction: Discord: custom epoch 2015, 42-bit ts / 5 worker / 5 process / 12 incr, JSON strings. Instagram: in-DB shard bits (41+13+10), no separate Snowflake service.
Ephemeral ZK without fencing or recycling IDs too fast after crash can duplicate. Hold leases past max clock skew so two nodes never share an ID in an overlapping window.

gotchas.trap: Treating IDs as privacy-preserving or volume-hiding perfectly
gotchas.correction: Timestamp leaks rough create time; per-ms sequence is not a global counter—better than auto-incr for hiding totals, not privacy-preserving.

gotchas.trap: Returning raw 64-bit IDs through JS/JSON numbers
gotchas.correction: IDs above 2^53-1 lose precision in JS Number; use string transport (Discord pattern).
